blocks.text: A healthy couple have a baby with cystic fibrosis. Neither parent has ever been ill, and no one in either family has the disease. Mendelian inheritance explains how two unaffected people can pass on a serious condition, and how to calculate the chance that it happens again.

blocks.markdown: Genes occur in pairs, one allele inherited from each parent. A **genotype** is the pair of alleles at a locus; the **phenotype** is the observable trait. A person with two identical alleles is **homozygous**; with different alleles, **heterozygous**. A **dominant** allele shows its effect in heterozygotes; a **recessive** allele shows only when homozygous. Single-gene (Mendelian) disorders are classified by the chromosome carrying the gene (autosomal or X-linked) and by the dominant or recessive behaviour.

rows: Affects every generation (vertical transmission); both sexes equally; an affected person has an affected parent (except new mutations); male-to-male transmission occurs; each child of an affected heterozygote has a 50% risk
Huntington disease; familial hypercholesterolaemia; Marfan syndrome; neurofibromatosis type 1
Often skips generations (horizontal pattern); both sexes equally; parents usually unaffected carriers; consanguinity increases risk
Cystic fibrosis; sickle cell disease; phenylketonuria
Mainly affects males; no male-to-male transmission; carrier mothers pass to sons; affected fathers pass the allele to all daughters (carriers)
Duchenne muscular dystrophy; haemophilia A; red-green colour blindness
Affects both sexes, more females; an affected father transmits to all daughters and no sons
blocks.caption: Mendelian patterns and how to recognise them from a pedigree.

blocks.title: Reading a pedigree
blocks.text: Squares are males, circles are females, filled symbols are affected individuals. Check three things: does the trait appear in every generation (dominant) or skip generations (recessive); does it affect both sexes equally (autosomal) or mainly males (X-linked); and is there any male-to-male transmission (which excludes X-linked inheritance)?

blocks.title: Identifying the pattern
blocks.prompt: A pedigree shows a trait in a grandfather, one of his three sons and two of that son's four children (a daughter and a son). The affected son's wife is unaffected. The grandfather's other sons are unaffected and have unaffected children. Which inheritance pattern fits and why?

steps.text: The trait appears in three consecutive generations: vertical transmission suggests a dominant pattern.
An affected father (the son) has an affected son, so male-to-male transmission occurs, excluding X-linked inheritance.
Both a daughter and a son are affected, so it affects both sexes: autosomal.
The unaffected parents of other branches have unaffected children, consistent with a dominant allele that has not been inherited by them.

blocks.markdown:
### Recurrence risk for carriers of a recessive condition

If both parents are heterozygous **carriers** (Aa x Aa) of an autosomal recessive allele, each parent transmits A or a with probability 1/2. The four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa, so each child has a **1 in 4 (25%) chance of being affected (aa)**, a 1 in 2 chance of being an unaffected carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. Importantly, **each pregnancy is independent**: previous affected children do not change the risk. An unaffected sibling of an affected child has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, since the 'aa' outcome is excluded and two of the remaining three outcomes are carriers.

blocks.caption: Both carrier parents must transmit the recessive allele; the two events are independent.

blocks.title: Two carriers, two children
blocks.prompt: Two known carriers of cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive) plan a family. (a) What is the risk that a given child is affected? (b) They already have one affected child; what is the risk for the next? (c) What is the probability that two children are both affected?

steps.text: (a) Each parent transmits the mutant allele with probability 1/2, so risk = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 = 25%.
(b) Conception is independent of previous outcomes, so the risk is again 1/4.

blocks.markdown:
### Trinucleotide repeat expansion and anticipation

Some disorders are caused by **expansion of unstable trinucleotide repeats** within or near genes. Examples: **CAG** repeats in Huntington disease (in the coding region, producing an expanded polyglutamine tract), **CGG** repeats in fragile X syndrome (in the 5' untranslated region, leading to methylation and silencing of FMR1) and **CTG** repeats in myotonic dystrophy. Normal alleles contain a few repeats; once the number exceeds a threshold the repeat becomes **unstable** and tends to expand when passed on through the germline (during gametogenesis, by slippage during DNA replication). Larger expansions cause earlier and more severe disease. This produces **anticipation**: in successive generations, the disease appears earlier and is more severe. In Huntington disease expansion occurs preferentially through paternal transmission, while in fragile X and myotonic dystrophy large expansions are usually passed on by the mother.

blocks.title: Explaining anticipation
blocks.prompt: A man with Huntington disease has 42 CAG repeats and develops symptoms at age 50. His son has 55 repeats and develops symptoms at 31. Explain.

steps.text: The CAG repeat tract is unstable; during spermatogenesis replication slippage can add repeats.
The son inherited an expanded allele (55 repeats), which is larger than the father's 42.
A longer polyglutamine tract produces more toxic protein, so onset is earlier. This is anticipation.

blocks.answer: Repeat expansion between generations increases severity and lowers age of onset.

items: Autosomal dominant disease may show variable expressivity and reduced penetrance.
Carrier frequency is higher than disease frequency in recessive conditions.
Other non-Mendelian patterns include mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance and genomic imprinting.
New (de novo) mutations can cause apparently sporadic dominant disease.

blocks.title: Independent events
blocks.text: The recurrence risk for two carriers is 25% for every pregnancy, regardless of previous children. Do not assume that having had an affected child makes the next one less likely.

points: Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation, autosomal recessive traits skip generations, and X-linked recessive traits mainly affect males with no male-to-male transmission.
Two carriers of an autosomal recessive allele have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child in every pregnancy.
Unstable trinucleotide repeats expand when transmitted, so successive generations show earlier and more severe disease (anticipation).

questions.stem: A pedigree shows an affected father with an affected son, and the trait appears in each generation affecting both sexes. Which pattern is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Vertical transmission through generations, both sexes affected and male-to-male transmission together indicate autosomal dominant inheritance.

questions.stem: A boy has haemophilia A. His parents and sisters are unaffected, and his maternal uncle has the same condition. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carrier mother, affected male relatives on the maternal side.
distractorRationale.c: Autosomal recessive would affect both sexes equally and not cluster in males.
distractorRationale.d: An X-linked dominant trait would affect the mother.

questions.explanation: Affected males linked through unaffected females (the mother carries the allele) fit X-linked recessive inheritance. Haemophilia A is the classic example.

questions.stem: An unaffected man whose sister has an autosomal recessive condition (his parents are both carriers) wants to know his own carrier risk. What is it?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aa is excluded because he is unaffected, leaving AA, Aa, aA.
distractorRationale.b: This ignores that he is unaffected.
distractorRationale.c: This is the risk of being affected.
distractorRationale.d: This is the chance he is not a carrier.

questions.explanation: Of the four equally likely outcomes, aa is excluded because he is unaffected, leaving three, of which two are carriers. His carrier risk is therefore 2/3.

questions.stem: Which statement about trinucleotide repeat disorders is correct?

options.text: Repeats above a threshold are unstable and tend to expand on transmission, giving earlier onset in later generations
They are always inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
They cause disease only when the repeat number is low

questions.correctOptionText: Repeats above a threshold are unstable and tend to expand on transmission, giving earlier onset in later generations

distractorRationale.c: Huntington disease is dominant, fragile X is X-linked.
distractorRationale.d: Disease arises with high repeat number.

questions.explanation: Expansion of unstable repeats through successive generations produces anticipation. Larger repeat numbers give earlier and more severe disease.

questions.stem: True or false: X-linked recessive disorders are never transmitted from father to son.
questions.explanation: Sons receive the Y chromosome from their father, so an X-linked allele cannot pass from father to son. Affected fathers pass the X-linked allele to all daughters.

questions.stem: Which disease is caused by a CGG repeat expansion in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 with methylation and gene silencing?

distractorRationale.b: Huntington disease is CAG in the coding region.
distractorRationale.c: Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR mutations.
distractorRationale.d: Duchenne is caused by dystrophin deletions.

questions.explanation: In fragile X syndrome, a CGG expansion leads to hypermethylation and silencing of FMR1. Huntington disease involves CAG repeats in a coding region.

questions.stem: Two phenylketonuria carriers (autosomal recessive) have three children. Calculate the probability, as a percentage, that all three children are affected.
questions.explanation: Each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected and births are independent, so (1/4)^3 = 1/64 = 0.015625, i.e. 1.56%. The previous outcomes do not alter the risk of any single child.

questions.stem: A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder and her partner is unaffected. How many percent of their sons are expected to be affected?
questions.explanation: A carrier mother transmits the mutant X to half of her children. Sons who receive it are affected because they have no second X, so 50% of sons are affected, and 50% of daughters are carriers.

questions.stem: A couple, both healthy, have a child with sickle cell disease. Explain how this can occur, give the recurrence risk and give the carrier risk for the healthy sibling of an affected child.
markingGuide: Autosomal recessive: both parents are heterozygous carriers
Each parent transmits mutant allele with probability 1/2: risk 1/4 (25%) per pregnancy
Risk is independent for each pregnancy
Healthy sibling: 2/3 chance of being a carrier
Mention of 1/4 unaffected non-carrier and 1/2 carrier
questions.explanation: Carriers are phenotypically normal, so disease appears unexpectedly. Probabilities follow from independent allele transmission.

questions.stem: Explain the molecular basis of anticipation in Huntington disease and how it differs from a simple point-mutation disorder.
markingGuide: CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin gene encoding polyglutamine
Repeats above threshold are unstable and expand during gametogenesis (replication slippage), especially paternal
Longer repeats cause more severe and earlier disease
Anticipation: earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations
Unlike a point mutation, the mutation size changes between generations
questions.explanation: The mutation itself changes during transmission, so phenotype worsens. A fixed point mutation would be passed unchanged.
